analysis.one_liner: Bans insurers from rejecting people for preexisting conditions and subsidizes coverage for low-income children and the temporarily unemployed.
analysis.headline: Introduced January 4, 1995 by 12 Senate Democrats and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, the bill never received a hearing or a vote before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This was a scaled-back health care reform bill introduced after the larger 1993-94 overhaul failed. It would have barred health insurers from denying coverage or setting premiums based on a person's health history, guaranteed people the right to enroll in and keep their plans, limited preexisting-condition exclusions to six months, and banned lifetime benefit caps. It would also have created federal subsidies for low-income children and briefly unemployed workers to buy private coverage, steadily increased the tax deduction for self-employed people's health insurance, and added rural telemedicine grants, national health-privacy rules, tighter fraud penalties, and limits on medical-malpractice awards. Its final title says none of it takes effect until Congress separately passes legislation making it budget-neutral.
analysis.who_benefits: People with preexisting conditions or chronic illnesses, who could no longer be refused coverage or charged based on health status; low-income children (starting at 133% of poverty in 1997, rising to 240% by 2001) and temporarily unemployed workers, who would get premium subsidies; self-employed people, whose health insurance deduction would rise from 25% to 100% by 1999; small employers and individual buyers, who would gain guaranteed enrollment and renewal plus grants for group purchasing pools; and rural residents, who would gain telemedicine grants and a senior rural-health office.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with preexisting conditions and low-income families

how_it_helps.text: Health plans could not deny, limit, or price coverage based on health status, medical history, disability, or claims experience, and had to guarantee enrollment and renewal to individuals and small employers.
Preexisting-condition exclusions would be capped at six months, reduced month-for-month by prior continuous coverage, and could not apply to pregnancy or newborns.
Lifetime benefit caps would be prohibited.
States would receive federal payments to give premium subsidies to low-income children and to workers briefly unemployed after at least six months of job-based coverage.
The self-employed health insurance deduction would rise from 25% to 50% in 1997, 75% in 1998, and 100% in 1999 and after.

States could get grants to build small-employer and individual purchasing pools, and plans would have to meet quality, consumer-protection, and access standards including public report cards and grievance procedures.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund the premium subsidies and grant programs; healthy, younger buyers in the small-group market, who would pay more as insurers are restricted from charging based on health and allowed to charge older adults up to three times the youngest age band; states, which would have to enforce the standards and run the subsidy programs; and malpractice plaintiffs, who would face caps on noneconomic damages and attorney fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and healthier insurance buyers

drawbacks.text: Title V bars any provision of the bill from taking effect until Congress separately enacts legislation making the bill budget-neutral, so it could pass and still do nothing.
The children's subsidy starts narrow (families up to 133% of poverty in 1997) and total federal payments are capped at a CBO estimate, with income limits adjusted downward if costs run over.
The malpractice title limits attorney contingency fees and noneconomic-damage awards and sends half of punitive damages to state programs, reducing compensation for people injured by negligent care.
Premiums could still vary by age up to a 3-to-1 ratio, so older working-age buyers could pay far more than the youngest enrollees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The insurance market rules — guaranteed issue and renewal, health-status nondiscrimination, portability credit, and an end to lifetime caps — are strong consumer protections that address the biggest ways people lose coverage. The cost is real but ordinary: healthier and younger buyers would pay somewhat more, and taxpayers would fund targeted subsidies. The bill's most serious flaw is self-inflicted: the budget-neutrality trigger means its protections are contingent on a second act of Congress that might never come, and its malpractice caps trade patient compensation for provider relief with little demonstrated offset.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on the Senate's first day of 1995, sent to the Finance Committee, and never heard from again — no hearing, no markup, no vote before the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Daschle introduced the bill on January 4, 1995, joined by eleven Democratic cosponsors including Kennedy, Reid, Rockefeller, and Breaux.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The only action after that was a 'star print' — a reprinting correction — ordered on January 11, 1995.
No hearing, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded; the 104th Congress ended January 3, 1997 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers spent two more years free to screen out sick applicants and cap lifetime benefits, and medical-malpractice plaintiffs kept the existing system. People with preexisting conditions gained nothing from this bill, though Congress later that Congress passed narrower insurance-portability rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and the malpractice status quo

for.name: Sen. Thomas Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 4, 1995 and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: 11 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Kennedy, Reid, Mikulski, Rockefeller, Dodd, Breaux, Moseley-Braun, Pell, Murray, Inouye)

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction in the Republican-majority Senate
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing or markup was ever scheduled, and the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors were Democrats, and the bill went to a Finance Committee controlled by the new Republican majority, which never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would impose real discipline — guaranteed issue and renewal, health-status nondiscrimination, rating limits, quality standards — but it also routes federal premium subsidies to low-income children and unemployed workers through private 'qualified health plans,' locking private insurers in as the channel for public health coverage dollars.

Providers would gain malpractice limits, antitrust safe harbors for rural collaboration, telemedicine grants, and Medicare reimbursement rules for telemedicine. The malpractice caps come at the expense of patients seeking compensation for negligent care, while the telemedicine and rural provisions expand access for rural patients.

Caps on contingency fees and noneconomic damages shrink malpractice litigation and fees. The same caps also limit recovery for genuinely injured patients, so the lawyers' loss and the patients' loss share a cause.

A rising tax deduction (to 100% by 1999) and grants for group purchasing pools would lower the cost of covering workers, addressing the small-business penalty in the individual and small-group insurance markets.
